chapter_theme: Natrinai 261 to 280: the friend at the hill and the shore turning night trysts, veri rites and slander into pressure for marriage; male birds that feed their pregnant mates on the neythal shore; a hero torn between his wife and the shame of poverty; two mothers whose daughters have eloped; a heroine who curses a bee for not carrying word; and a wife who has no time to sulk because her house, like the Velir's Kunrur, is always full of guests.

261.reading: The friend, knowing the man stands within hearing, tells the girl he has no pity: he comes at midnight in the heavy rain, when lightning splits the dark sky and thunder roars over the many tall hills, by the narrow path of the great rock where a raging python that has caught an elephant coils round a hard-cored tree and wrenches it, past caves fragrant with sandal and tall eruvai flowers.
261.nuance: 'He has no grace' is said of a man who risks his life to come: the complaint is the friend's way of telling him, overhearing, that the night tryst must end and the only safe road is marriage. The python crushing the elephant gives the hearer the path's danger in one picture.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி இரவுக்குறி விலக்கி வரைவு கடாயது தலைமகள் இயற்பட மொழிந்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: hill paths at midnight in the rains fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: on this reading 'he has no grace' is the girl's fond complaint in his favour

262.reading: The hero tells his heart that she is already wasting: in the midnight of the sleeping town, when the north wind sways the great karuvilai flowers like the feathers of a dancing peacock, a trembling sickness thins her beauty; yet even if the heart, set on effort, says it will leave this girl with flower-scented hair and honeyed speech, the shame of having nothing is hard to bear.
262.nuance: The poem ends on the other side of the scale: the last line, about the shame of poverty, is the argument for going, and the colophon reads the whole as his checking his departure. He imagines her suffering in a future night as if it were already present.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் ஆற்றாக் குறிப்பு அறிந்து பிரிவிடை விலக்கியது

thinai_evidence.note: the parting for effort, not the scene, decides paalai

comparisons.tenor: the karuvilai flowers, shaped like eyes
the flowers swaying in the north wind

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the poem's பிரிவல் நெஞ்சு makes it the hero to his heart

263.reading: Overheard by the man, the friend tells the girl that though they never speak of it to him, out of shame, the forehead that has lost its crescent beauty, the bangles that slip from her wrist and the gossip of the town, her kohled tears, hidden again and again, have overflowed and told it all at the sight of the gentle lonely shore where an old lame stork, hunting, carries sea fish to his hen who, heavy with young, stays back in the field.
263.nuance: The tears 'speak' though the women do not: the friend makes the girl's body the messenger, so that the man hears a demand without being addressed.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: the stork fishing the sea by the shore grove fixes neythal

iraicchi.act: the old lame stork goes hunting and brings sea fish to his pregnant hen, who cannot reach the shore
iraicchi.sense: even a crippled old bird provides for the mate who carries his young; the man, whole and young, has not even married the girl he has made to suffer

264.reading: Leading the girl away with him, the man urges her on: the rain has poured with thunder that drives snakes into their holes, the morning is lovely, and she walks with the wind stirring her flower-strewn hair like a peacock with a sapphire neck spreading its bright tail; the day is ending, so go on, girl, for listen, the clear bells on the cows the cowherds have tied in the bamboo thicket are ringing, and there is our small good town.
264.nuance: The road of elopement, which paalai poems fill with heat and danger, is here a rain-washed mullai evening, and the end of it is not a wilderness but 'our town' with its cow-bells: the man reassures her by showing her the home she is coming to.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகாநின்ற தலைமகன் தலைமகளை வற்புறீஇயது உடன்போய் மறுத்தரா நின்றான் ஊர்காட்டி வற்புறீஇயதும் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the elopement journey is paalai's parting, whatever the landscape

comparisons.tenor: the girl walking with her hair stirred by the wind

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: bringing her back after the elopement, he shows her the town

265.reading: The man who has followed the girl tells his heart that her thick soft hair, precious as Paaram that Minjili, chief of the bowmen whose whistling arrows bring down the spotted stag, guards, as the town of the Chola with the small sceptre, and like the plumage of the joyous peacocks on Kolli, the hill of Ori whose giving is like the rain, is now ours.
265.nuance: Each comparison is a guarded or famous possession of a chief, so the girl's hair is praised as a prize won from the strongholds of the hill; the poem has no main verb as we have it, and the sense of the Chenni line is not certain.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகன் நெஞ்சிற்கு உரைத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill stag, the peacock of Kolli and the cleared hill field fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the girl's hair, a guarded prize

266.reading: The friend tells the man that they are folk of a small village on the wide land where, by the cowherds' little field, the short-stemmed kuravam blooms its clustered white flowers for the goatherd to wear, and that is enough for them; but besides love, if he leaves them she will say one thing: if a man flees once she has been made to live apart from her own people, is that not a great thing to say of the great?
266.nuance: The village's contentment with wild kuravam flowers is the friend's claim that they ask for no wealth, so the only reason to leave is his own; the last line praises 'the great' in a way that shames him.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகனைச் செலவுடன்பட்டது கடிநகர் வரைப்பில் கண்டு மகிழ்ந்த தலைமகற்குத் தோழி நும்மாலே ஆயிற்று என்று சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: cowherds, the goatherd and the kuravam of the forest fields fix mullai

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the poem's ஐய and எம் give the friend

267.reading: The friend, speaking where the man can hear, says that she would not have come to the sweet grove where the lord of the shore, whose crowds of crabs with eyes like nochchi buds scratch at fragrant njaazhal flowers as women with shining teeth stir drying millet with their hands, first met the girl, since coming there alone is so lonely; yet she came, and before she could say that the cries of the birds swarming over the shoals of fish, like the clear sound of small-tongued bells, were no man, he appeared there, strong as a lion.
267.nuance: The friend pretends the grove is haunted only by memory and birds, then lets the man's sudden arrival end the poem: the meeting place is still in use, and with the guard tightened, that is the reason to marry.

colophon.thurai: தோழி காப்புக் கைமிக்குக் காமம் பெருகிய காலத்துச் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது வரைவு கடாயதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: crabs of the dunes, njaazhal and the shore grove fix neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

occasion.words: காப்புக் கைமிக்குக் காமம் பெருகிய காலத்துச் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the girl is the likely hearer

268.reading: Of the man of the land where, in the tall hills, heavy rain fills the springs of the haunted wide places and the honey of the black-stemmed kurinji's pure white flowers oozes in hives built at the rock's edge as if painted, the speaker asks why the love he made has become unlove: let us ask, friend, by guarding the sand-strewn courtyard and bringing the velan with his molucca beans.
268.nuance: The veri rite is meant to name the god who has seized the girl; turning it to the question 'why has his love failed?' mocks the rite and points, past the velan, to the man as the real cause.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது தலைமகன் வந்தொழுகவும் வேறுபாடு கண்டாள் அவன் வருவானாகவும் நீ வேறுபட்டாய் வெறி எடுத்துக் கொள்ளும் வகையான் என்றதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the kurinji flower, hill honey and the velan's rite fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the honeycombs built on the rock

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend tells her the mother will hold a veri because she has changed though the man keeps coming

269.reading: Refusing the man entry, the friend reminds him of his son with bead-jewels and a big red anklet, his milky coral mouth, who climbs down his chest on the evening bed, and of the wife dear as their own life, with lovely teeth and a fine smile and blameless ways, whose eyes rove over his face, who binds him every day like the valli creeper; men who cross the many small hills do not think of that, and who knows what they intend?
269.nuance: The friend never says 'do not go': she sets the bed, the child and the wife's gaze before him and ends on a question about 'those who cross the hills', talking of him in the third person as if he were already gone.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வாயில் மறுத்தது செலவு அழுங்குவித்ததூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the crossing of the hills for gain is paalai's parting

270.reading: Letting the husband in, the friend tells him with irony that he has been far kinder to her than to the girl of broad shoulders who knows only how to adorn herself and not how to bind him, while the other woman with dark hair fragrant of the screwpine comes rolling to their side like a toy wheel; his cruelty is worse than the cruelty Nannan, the spear-lifting king of fine maned horses who routed kings, did to a woman's hair, and she will never forget his valour.
270.nuance: The praise of his valour and the comparison with Nannan's notorious cruelty turn the friend's consent into a rebuke: she lets him in by naming what he has done.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வாயில் நேர்கின்றாள் தலைமகனை நெருங்கிச் சொல்லி வாயில் எதிர்கொண்டது உடனிலைக் கிளவி வகையால்

thinai_evidence.note: the friend's sarcasm to a straying husband is marutham's sulking

comparisons.tenor: the other woman's coming to their side

occasion.words: தோழி வாயில் நேர்கின்றாள் தலைமகனை நெருங்கிச் சொல்லி வாயில் எதிர்கொண்டது

271.reading: A mother, bewildered in her house, says her daughter with kohled lily eyes has left the rich cool house, where the big-eared calf of the dark buffalo sleeps on fresh dung, to go with a bold youth, deceived by his lies, to a far land, eating with him the fallen gooseberries of the impassable grove and drinking the little water of flower-strewn springs; while her playmates, girls of her age who cut palm-leaf toys, go home in the evening moonlight, she asks that the great dark urn cover her and curses Death for passing her by.
271.nuance: The calf asleep by its mother at home stands against the daughter who has gone, and the playmates returning at evening measure her absence; the mother's grief turns into a wish to be buried.

colophon.thurai: மனை மருண்டு சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's journey to a far land through hard groves is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no addressee; the mother speaks aloud in the house

272.reading: The girl, worn by his long visits without marriage, says that the lord of the shore, where the red-beaked sea crow searches the flowered pool of the clear backwater for ayirai fish of the dark mud to feed his lovely hen resting heavy with young on a strip of white sand among the adumbu that ascetic women have stripped, has not been kind; her hope has come to nothing, her helplessness is in many mouths in the old town of gossip, and that has become a sickness greater than the sickness.
272.nuance: 'Greater than the sickness' ranks the pains: love-sickness she can bear, the town's talk she cannot, which is the reason the friend wants the man to hear.

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்தொழுக ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் சொல்லியது தோழி தலைமகளுக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய் தலைமகன் கேட்பச் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the sea crow fishing the backwater fixes neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

occasion.words: வரையாது நெடுங்காலம் வந்தொழுக ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; the friend is the likely hearer

iraicchi.act: the male sea crow searches the backwater pool for fish to feed his hen resting heavy with young
iraicchi.sense: a crow provides for the mate it has made pregnant, while the man of the same shore leaves the girl he has taken neither married nor cared for

273.reading: The friend, knowing the man has come, tells the girl, so that he may hear, that the mother, not knowing about them and troubled by the fearful suffering spreading through her body, will hear the velan call it the god's seizure; and her heart trembles whenever she thinks of the man of the hill country, where a lordly elephant drinks at a deep spring and the cool blue lily like her eyes grows fragrant.
273.nuance: Announcing the veri within his hearing is the friend's lever: if the rite is held the secret will come out, and only marriage forestalls it.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகனது வரவு உணர்ந்து தலைமகட்கு உரைப்பாளாய் நின் வேறுபாடு தாய்க்குப் புலனாக அவள் வேலனைக் கூவி வெறி அயரும் என்பது படச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man, the velan and the mountain spring fix kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the blue lily of his hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon's தலைமகனது வரவு உணர்ந்து implies he overhears

274.reading: The friend tells the girl that the man who once asked her to come with him through the hills where rain has poured from the lightning of the tall sky, where a doe brushing past scatters the bright kumizh fruits like gold coins on the many short paths, has now changed and crossed the wasteland of great rocks where the tiger roams in the groves: does he still have such words to say?
274.nuance: The rains that should bring him home only remind her of the invitation he made in the same season; the friend's question sets his old words against his present absence.

colophon.thurai: தோழி பருவம் மாறுபட்டது

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone across the wasteland makes it paalai

275.reading: Overheard by the man, the girl answers her friend's comfort: to the lord of the great-water shore, where a simple neythal flower, cut with its stalk by red-paddy reapers with sharp sickles who did not see it, lies among the sheaves and, not knowing its own ruin, slowly opens its fresh mouth to the burning sun as if waking from sweet sleep, she would not remember or grieve; even if that graceless man praised her she could bear it, she says, but in vain.
275.nuance: The -மன் of வல்லேன்மன் makes the boast hollow: she knows she cannot hold out, and the flower opening its face to the sun that will kill it is her own case.

colophon.thurai: சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகனது வரவுணர்ந்து வற்புறுப்ப வன்புறை எதிர்மொழிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower and the great-water shore fix neythal

ullurai.tenor: the girl, ruined by the man and still turning to him

pairs.situation: she was taken unawares by one who did not care what he cut
she does not yet own the harm done to her

pairs.scene: தெறு கதிர் இன் துயில் பசு வாய் திறக்கும்
pairs.situation: she still opens to the man who scorches her

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the neythal flower of her own shore and the paddy harvest she sees (porul 7.26)

276.reading: The friend tells the man who leaves after a daytime meeting that if he takes them for daughters of hunters who hunt the strong beast that rests after searching the forest with fierce dogs, they are only daughters of the hill folk, girls of the hill; their village is among the rocks, where the forest peacock nests on the high-legged platform the watchman built; so he should not go, but stay and go later, drinking the toddy matured in the curved bamboo of the great hill and watching the kuravai dance in the courtyard under the vengai.
276.nuance: Under 'the ways of the world' the colophon names, the friend offers the hill's hospitality, toddy and dance, to a man who comes only by day and leaves: an invitation to be received openly in the village, which is to say, to marry.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து பெயரும் தலைமகனை உலகியல் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: hill women, the vengai, the peacock and bamboo toddy fix kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

occasion.words: பகற்குறி வந்து பெயரும் தலைமகனை உலகியல் சொல்லியது

thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no speaker; the poem's we-forms give the friend

277.reading: The girl, whose lover went far for wealth without marrying her, tells the bee it is cruel and wishes her sickness on it: besides its black body, is its mind black too? It sucks the pollen-rich peeram flowers on the fine-thorned hedge of the well-guarded house but will not touch her pallor, the same yellow, because it has no scent; she has cared for it, and it brings her nothing; let it go to the loveless men who crossed the hard hot hills, tell them her state, and come back.
277.nuance: The yellow peeram and the yellow pallor are set side by side: the bee can tell them apart only by smell, and so cannot be made to carry the one that matters.

colophon.thurai: பட்ட பின்றை வரையாது கிழவோன் நெட்டிடைக் கழிந்து பொருள்வயிற் பிரியஆற்றளாகிய தலைமகள் தும்பிக்குச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the man gone across hot wastelands for gain makes it paalai

comparisons.tenor: her pallor, the same yellow, which the bee will not touch

278.reading: The friend tells the girl that she now knows the lord of the shore, where the broad-trunked punnai's buds open like bubbles, its gold-like pollen-laden flowers are what garland-makers left over, and green ghee-rich fruit hangs from every branch, is to be her husband: the red prawns have shrunk away even under the hooves of the thick-legged mules that splashed in the backwater mud, and the garlands are all white sand in the north wind.
278.nuance: The proof is in the mud: tracks of many mules on the shore mean a large party has come, the kind that comes to ask for a bride.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகட்கு வரைவு மலிந்தது

thinai_evidence.note: punnai, backwater mud and prawns fix neythal

279.reading: The mother whose daughter has gone off with her lover asks whether the feet of her jewelled girl, whose anklets were taken off and who has gone to another's house, are weary struggling on the path through a wasteland that glitters in the sun's heat, where bats, tired of neem fruit and craving the sweet milky iluppai, drip cold drops from every branch like ghee from a wick, and a hungry she-elephant has kicked the red bark of the omai tree.
279.nuance: The removal of the anklets (சிலம்பு கழீஇய) was the rite before marriage; the mother names it as the one wealth of a girl who has gone to marry elsewhere, so the poem grieves both the road and the wedding she did not see.

colophon.thurai: மகட் போக்கிய தாய் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the sun-scorched wasteland path fixes paalai

comparisons.tenor: the drops dripping from the bats
the kicked bark of the omai

thurai_akam.speaker: nartaay
thurai_akam.note: no addressee; the mother speaks to herself

280.reading: The wife tells the friend who asks her not to sulk at the man of the cool-ford town, where the sweet fruit the stork missed falls with a plop into the deep pool among water-lily buds shaped like a stork's hunched stance, for his endless philandering, that she will not sulk: her good house, like Kunrur of the ancient Velir where field guards break curly snails on the green-mossed back of the field turtle, is so busy feasting guests that she has no leisure for it.
280.nuance: The refusal is a sulk in itself: 'I have no time to sulk' says that she has the house, the guests and the standing, and he has nothing she needs. The fruit missed by the stork that drops among stork-shaped buds hints at favours falling to the women who look like the wife, but it does not give two clear pairs.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் மறுத்து மொழிந்தது தலைமகனை ஏற்றுக்கொண்டு வழிபட்டாளைப் புகழ்ந்து புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉம் ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk at a philandering husband is marutham

comparisons.vehicle: கொக்கின் கூம்பு நிலை அன்ன முகைய ஆம்பல்

comparisons.tenor: her good house, full of guests

occasion.words: வாயில் வேண்டிச் சென்ற தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் மறுத்து மொழிந்தது
தலைமகனை ஏற்றுக்கொண்டு வழிபட்டாளைப் புகழ்ந்து புக்க தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியதூஉம்

links.note: Kural 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words; Natrinai 262's man, seeing his wife already wasting, ends on 'hard indeed is the shame of having nothing' (இன்மையது இளிவே).
links.teaches: The Natrinai shows what Valluvar's shame of poverty weighs against in a man's life: it is the one argument strong enough to set beside a wife's midnight suffering, so the couplet's social fear turns out to be the engine of the paalai parting.

links.note: Both are the man arguing with his heart over leaving his wife for wealth; in Akananuru 199 he refuses even riches like the land Narmudi Cheral won back, in Natrinai 262 he ends on the unbearable shame of poverty, which on the plain reading tips him toward going.
links.teaches: Read together they show that the debate with the heart had no fixed outcome in the tradition: the same scene of the wife's shoulders could close either way, and what decides each poem is the argument the poet places last.

links.note: Both are neythal poems about a man who will not marry: in 263 an old lame stork brings sea fish to his pregnant hen in the field, in 272 a red-beaked sea crow searches the backwater for fish for his hen heavy with young on the sand.
links.teaches: Two poets put the same act, a male shore bird feeding its pregnant mate, beside the same complaint, so the provider bird was a conventional reproach that let the women shame an unmarried lover without naming his fault.

links.note: Both are Paranar's, both the man speaking to his heart after meeting the girl: in Akananuru 152 her shoulders are like the plumage of the joyous peacock on the Ezhil hill of Nannan, lord of Paaram; in Natrinai 265 her hair is like the plumage of the joyous peacock (கலி மயில் கலாவத்து) on Ori's Kolli, and Paaram, guarded by Minjili, is another of her measures.
links.teaches: The pair shows Paranar keeping one formula, a chief's hill peacock, for the girl and changing only the chief, and Akananuru 152 supplies the Paaram-Nannan link that makes sense of the elliptic 265: her beauty is ranked among the guarded possessions of the hill chiefs.

links.note: Akananuru 208, also Paranar's man speaking to his heart after union, tells of Minjili's war at Paazhi and ends on her hair fragrant as the flowers of Ori's Kolli; Natrinai 265 names Minjili guarding Paaram and Ori's Kolli in its run of comparisons for her hair.
links.teaches: The longer poem tells the war story behind the names that the short one only lists, so Natrinai 265's Minjili is not a decorative name but the victor of a battle Paranar's audience knew, and the girl is measured against fame won in war.

links.note: Both are, on Parimelazhagar's reading of the Kural, the friend trying to stop the man's departure: Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return to those who will still be alive; Natrinai 269 sets before him his son climbing down his chest and his wife's eyes on his face.
links.teaches: The pair shows two opposite tactics for one thurai, the Kural's friend making the woman's death the stake and the Natrinai's friend making the man's own pleasures at home the stake, so the couplet's threat is one option among the friend's arguments, not the only one.

links.note: Both are Paranar's and both use Nannan's cruelty to a woman as a measure: Kuruntokai 292 curses the mother to go to hell like Nannan who killed a girl for eating a fruit; Natrinai 270 tells the husband his cruelty is worse than Nannan's to a woman's hair.
links.teaches: Holding them together shows that Paranar made one king's notorious offence against a woman into a standing scale for cruelty in love, turned in one poem on a guarding mother and in the other on a straying husband.

links.note: Both are about a mother whose daughter has eloped: Akananuru 165, seen by onlookers, has a calf drinking at the buffalo in the old town, the playmates mourning and the mother crying 'let my life end'; Natrinai 271, in the mother's own voice, has a buffalo calf asleep on the dung of the house, the playmates going home at evening and her curse on Death for not taking her.
links.teaches: The two poems share an inventory for the house a daughter has left (the buffalo calf beside its mother, the girl's playmates, the mother's wish to die), which shows these were the fixed signs of that grief and lets the calf safe beside its dam be read as the daughter who did not stay.

links.note: Both are neythal poems of a girl neglected by the lord of the shore with the sea crow and its 'lovely hen' (காமர் பேடை, காமர் பெடை): in Akananuru 170 the small sea crow rests with its mate while she is alone at midnight, in Natrinai 272 the crow fishes for its pregnant mate while the man is not kind.
links.teaches: The pair shows the shore crow with its mate measuring the man's neglect in two ways, by companionship in the one and by provision in the other, so the bird's pairing was a flexible yardstick for whatever the girl lacks.

links.note: Both have the friend speak to the girl while the man overhears about the mother who, not knowing the cause, will bring the velan to hold a veri; in Akananuru 242 the friend says they should go to him before the goat is offered, in Natrinai 273 the poem ends on her trembling heart.
links.teaches: Together they show the announced veri as a set lever on the overhearing man, the false diagnosis that will expose the secret, and Akananuru 242 states the remedy, his embrace before the sacrifice, that Natrinai 273 leaves him to supply.

links.note: Both carry the thurai of the friend disputing the season of his return: in Kuruntokai 66 the konrai are foolish to take the untimely rain for his season; in Natrinai 274 the rain has come and she asks whether the man who invited the girl along the rain-washed hills has those words now.
links.teaches: The pair shows two ways to deny the season: Kuruntokai 66 blames the trees and so keeps faith in his promise, while Natrinai 274 sets his own old words against the rain and so doubts him, so the same thurai could comfort or accuse.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 2 the man asks the bee, knower of flowers, whether any is more fragrant than her hair; in Natrinai 277 the woman curses the bee for sucking the yellow peeram but not her yellow pallor, because it has no scent, and asks it to carry word to her man.
links.teaches: Akam's bee is a judge of scent, and the pair shows the limit of that office: it can testify to a beloved's beauty in union but cannot be made to carry the scentless pallor of separation, which is why the girl's appeal to it fails.

links.note: Both have the girl, with no human messenger, beg a creature to go to her man: in Akananuru 170 the crab, since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak; in Natrinai 277 the bee, after she scolds it.
links.teaches: Together they show the creature-messenger as the last resort of a girl who cannot speak openly, and Natrinai 277 adds the grievance that the creature has its own pleasures to prefer, so the appeal is also a complaint that even the messenger neglects her.

links.note: Kural 81 says the whole of keeping a house is for tending guests; in Natrinai 280 the wife, urged not to sulk at her philandering husband, says she cannot even sulk because her house, like the Velir's Kunrur, is never free of feasting guests.
links.teaches: The Natrinai shows the Kural's household duty turned into a weapon in love: hospitality is a reason no one can fault, so the wife uses it to refuse both the sulk and the husband, and the virtue becomes the frame of her pride.

source_issues: Natrinai colophons give speaker, addressee and occasion in prose; where they name no speaker or addressee (262, 266, 267, 268, 271, 272, 276, 277, 279) thurai_akam supplies one from the poem, with a note.
262: the colophon names no speaker; the poem is the hero speaking to his heart (பிரிவல் நெஞ்சு என்னும்), so the speaker is coded thalaivan, addressee nenju.

268: the colophon says the poem is spoken to the heroine, but the poem's own vocative is தோழி (line 7) and the speaker proposes to question the velan herself; on the poem's evidence the heroine may be the speaker. Kept as the colophon has it.
270: the colophon thinai is நெய்தல்; the screwpine is a shore thing, but the situation is the friend's sarcasm to a husband who wanders (oodal), so I infer marutham.
271: the colophon gives no poet (text flag).
277: the colophon's பொருள்வயிற் பிரியஆற்றளாகிய looks like a misprint for பிரிய ஆற்றாளாகிய.

262 line 2, 275 line 3, 279 line 5: the lost -ஒடு vowel sign restored (text flag); 267 line 9: TSCII repair read as தெள் with tamilvu.org; 273 line 1: ஃ restored; 276 line 1: நாயொடு restored by rule and not confirmed by sangamtamil.com.

265 is syntactically incomplete as we have it (a run of comparisons ending in நம் வயினானே with no main verb), and the sense of சிறு கோற் சென்னி ஆரேற்றன்ன is not clear to me; 270 lines 1 to 5 and 279 lines 5 to 7 are also hard to construe.
